implementation_notes: Swift ships the exchange: swap(&a, &b) exchanges two inout values through an internal temporary (no allocation, no user code, no throw - the standard library implementation moves with Builtin.take), and MutableCollection.swapAt(i, j) is the collection form introduced together with the Law of Exclusivity, because swap(&array[i], &array[j]) performs two overlapping write accesses to the same variable. Value types with copy-on-write storage make exchanging a large value O(1) - the buffer reference moves, the contents do not - which is exactly the handle swap the pattern describes, and the standard library documents swap as requiring its two arguments not to alias. The remaining discipline is to keep the exchanged state behind one reference and to do the fallible work before it.
pitfalls: swap(&array[i], &array[j]) is an exclusivity violation (two overlapping write accesses to the same array) and is diagnosed by the compiler; use array.swapAt(i, j).

swap requires that its two arguments do not alias - the standard library states the precondition and traps when it is violated (the older implementation even carried an explicit self-swap precondition).

For a class the exchange swaps references, not contents: swap(&obj.a, &obj.b) mutates the object that other references share, whereas only a var handle can be rebound, so keep state in one handle when the commit must be observable as a whole.
Exchanging a struct that owns many inline fields copies them field by field; put bulk state behind an Array, Dictionary or class reference so the exchange stays O(1) and runs no ARC traffic mid-swap.
